title: Spatial and Temporal Trends of Nitellopsis obtusa in Coastal Wetlands of the Laurentian Great Lakes: Implications for Conservation and Management
content:
ABSTRACT

The invasive macroalga, Nitellopsis obtusa (‘N. obtusa’), commonly known as starry stonewort, is rapidly expanding across North American freshwater systems. This study assessed the spatial distribution and abundance of N. obtusa over time in coastal wetlands of the Laurentian Great Lakes (hereafter ‘Great Lakes’) using data collected from the Great Lakes Coastal Wetland Monitoring Program. In this study, a total of 511 wetlands were compared across two 5-year sampling cycles (2015–2019 and 2020–2024). The number of wetlands in the Great Lakes with N. obtusa increased significantly from 8% of wetland sites in 2015–2019 to 15% in 2020–2024. Lake Ontario exhibited a significant increase in site-level detections (25% to 31%). While Lake Superior and Lake Huron had no detections in the first sampling cycle, new occurrences were documented in the second. Lake Michigan and Lake Erie showed no significant change in the number of sites with N. obtusa between the two sampling cycles. Quadrat-level analyses revealed similar patterns; the number of quadrats with N. obtusa increased significantly across the Great Lakes, along with the number of quadrats where N. obtusa covered ≥ 50% of the quadrat. Notably, Lake Ontario experienced significant increases in the number of quadrats with N. obtusa present and high-cover quadrats (≥ 50%), whereas Lake Erie showed no significant changes overall. These findings suggest rapid colonization and proliferation of this invasive species. This study highlights key areas for future monitoring and emphasizes the importance of coordinated management strategies, early detection and more awareness to support the conservation of Great Lakes wetland ecosystems.
